# Bubble charts {#sec-bubble-charts} ::: {.callout-tip appearance='simple' icon=false} ***This graph is largely complete and just needs final proof reading.*** ::: :::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false}
::: {.cell layout-align="right"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](bubble_charts_files/figure-html/full_code_display-1.png){fig-align='right' width=60% height=60%} ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"} **Requirements:** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ three numeric (continuous) variables** ::: :::: ## Description Bubble graphs display relationships between three numeric (continuous) variables. The position on the `x` and `y` axis illustrates the relationship between the first two variables, and the `size` of the point (i.e., the bubble) conveys the numeric value of the third. ## Set up ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **PACKAGES:** ::: Install packages. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DATA:** ::: *Seinfeld* was famously a show about nothing, and every episode got a bump whenever Kramer slid through Jerry's door. We'll simulate 180 episodes across nine seasons (20 per season) with three numeric variables: - `kramer_minutes`: Kramer's screen time, drawn from a right skewed gamma distribution with `rgamma()` - `laughs_per_min`: the studio audience's laughs per minute, which go up 0.3 for every minute of Kramer (plus noise from `rnorm()`) - `viewers`: the audience in millions, which grows by about 3 million each season. We draw these on the log scale with `rnorm()` and convert them back with `exp()` Setting the seed with `set.seed()` means you'll get the same 180 episodes every time you run the code below. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} set.seed(1989) seinfeld_eps <- tibble( episode = 1:180, season = rep(1:9, each = 20)) |> mutate( kramer_minutes = round(rgamma(n(), shape = 6, rate = 1.5), 1), laughs_per_min = round(2 + 0.3 * kramer_minutes + rnorm(n(), mean = 0, sd = 0.5), 1), viewers = round(exp(rnorm(n(), mean = log(10 + 3 * (season - 1)), sd = 0.15)), 1)) glimpse(seinfeld_eps) #> Rows: 180 #> Columns: 5 #> $ episode 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9… #> $ season 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1… #> $ kramer_minutes 5.6, 5.6, 1.4, 2.7, 3.1, … #> $ laughs_per_min 3.8, 2.0, 2.4, 2.7, 3.0, … #> $ viewers 13.8, 10.6, 10.8, 8.2, 10… ``` ::: ::: ## Distribution A bubble chart adds a third variable to a scatter plot with the size of each point. Our eyes read the *area* of a bubble, not its width, so how a value gets turned into a size matters as much as the value itself. Below we'll move from the viewers, to a picture, to the formula. ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **COUNT IT:** ::: Start with the first five episodes. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} head(seinfeld_eps, 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: Below we summarise the `viewers` for each season. The mean grows each season, and so does the standard deviation, but their ratio (`cv`) stays close to 0.15. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} seinfeld_seasons <- seinfeld_eps |> group_by(season) |> summarise(mean_viewers = mean(viewers), sd_viewers = sd(viewers), cv = sd_viewers / mean_viewers) seinfeld_seasons ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DRAW IT:** ::: The graph below draws three bubbles for 10, 20, and 40 million viewers, two ways. On the left, `scale_size()` makes the *area* of each bubble proportional to the value (so 40 million looks four times bigger than 10 million). On the right, `scale_radius()` makes the *width* proportional to the value, and 40 million looks sixteen times bigger than 10 million. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} three_bubbles <- tibble(x = 1:3, y = 1, viewers = c(10, 20, 40)) ggplot(three_bubbles, aes(x = x, y = y, size = viewers)) + geom_point(color = "#F7C33C") + scale_size(range = c(0, 20), limits = c(0, 40)) + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.5, 3.5)) + labs(title = "scale_size()", x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "none", axis.text = element_blank()) ggplot(three_bubbles, aes(x = x, y = y, size = viewers)) + geom_point(color = "#F7C33C") + scale_radius(range = c(0, 20), limits = c(0, 40)) + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.5, 3.5)) + labs(title = "scale_radius()", x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "none", axis.text = element_blank()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](bubble_charts_files/figure-html/draw_bubble-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](bubble_charts_files/figure-html/draw_bubble-2.png){width=576} ::: ::: ::: `scale_size()` is the default for `size` in `ggplot2`, and it's the right choice for bubble charts. ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **NAME IT:** ::: The viewers come from a [lognormal distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log-normal_distribution) (normal on the log scale), with a median that grows each season: $$ \log(\text{viewers}) \sim \text{Normal}\left(\log(10 + 3(\text{season} - 1)), \; 0.15\right) $$ On the log scale every season has the same spread (0.15), which is why the `cv` stays near 0.15 in every season: a lognormal variable wobbles by about the same *percent*, not the same number of viewers. When we map `viewers` to `size`, `scale_size()` sets each bubble's area in proportion to its value: $$ \text{area} \propto \text{viewers}, \quad \text{radius} \propto \sqrt{\text{viewers}} $$ A season nine episode with about 34 million viewers gets a bubble about 3.2 times the area of a season one episode (10 million), but only about 1.8 times as wide. Try changing `sd = 0.15` to `sd = 0.5` and the bubbles within each season range from tiny to huge. ## Grammar ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **CODE:** ::: - Create labels with `labs()` - Map `kramer_minutes` to `x` axis - Map `laughs_per_min` to `y` axis - Map `viewers` to `size` - Set `alpha` to `1/3` - Add `scale_size()`, set the `range` to `c(0.1, 10)` and `name` to `"Viewers (millions)"` - Move the legend to the bottom of the graph with `theme(legend.position = "bottom")` ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} labs_bubble <- labs( title = "Seinfeld episodes", subtitle = "Kramer's screen time vs. laughs per minute", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Kramer screen time (minutes)", y = "Laughs per minute", size = "Viewers (millions)") ggp2_bubble <- seinfeld_eps |> ggplot( aes(x = kramer_minutes, y = laughs_per_min)) + geom_point(aes(size = viewers), alpha = 1/3) + scale_size(range = c(.1, 10), name = "Viewers (millions)") + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ggp2_bubble + labs_bubble ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **GRAPH:** ::: ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](bubble_charts_files/figure-html/create_graph_bubble-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: :::
